questions.q: What specifically breaks when logs are free text instead of structured, at production scale?
options: Free-text logs can no longer be written to disk at all
A precise query across millions of lines degrades into a fragile regular expression that breaks when message wording changes
Free-text logs cannot include a timestamp
Structured logs are always slower to write than free text
questions.explain: The problem isn't readability — it's queryability. Pattern-matching prose doesn't scale and breaks the moment someone rewords a log message.

questions.q: What does structured logging mean, as defined in this lesson?
options: Writing every log line as a well-defined data structure, usually JSON, with named fields instead of a freeform sentence
Writing logs only in all capital letters for consistency
Storing logs exclusively in a relational database table
Removing timestamps from log lines to save space
questions.explain: Structured logging emits the same facts a free-text line would, but at named, indexable fields — so a log backend can filter and group on them directly.

questions.q: Why does the trace_id field matter more than almost any other field in a structured log line?
options: It is required by law in financial logging systems
It replaces the need for a timestamp entirely
It is the only field that can be indexed by a log backend
It ties every log line from one request together and connects those logs back to that request's distributed trace
questions.explain: trace_id is the hinge between pillars — it lets you jump from a slow span in a trace straight to the exact log lines that request produced.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between the event field and the human-readable message in a structured log line?
options: The event field is only used in DEBUG-level logs
There is no difference; they always contain identical text
The event field is a stable, machine-friendly name for what happened that survives even if the surrounding message wording changes later
The event field replaces the trace_id field
questions.explain: Separating a stable event name from prose means downstream queries and alerts keep working even after someone edits the human-readable message text.

questions.q: Why is choosing a log level described as a decision rather than a default?
options: Because log levels only exist in cloud-native applications
Because every log line must legally be marked FATAL
Because the level is purely cosmetic and has no effect on tooling
Because the level controls what downstream tooling filters, samples, and alerts on — logging everything at INFO leaves grep as the only effective filter left
questions.explain: ERROR, WARN, INFO, and DEBUG each carry different operational meaning; defaulting everything to INFO erases that signal and bloats storage costs.
